references.text: The psalmist confesses that God knows his thoughts from afar, which points to Jesus' ability to know people's thoughts.
The Lord says that he searches the heart and tests the kidneys, showing that knowing the thoughts of the heart is a divine attribute—the same one Jesus demonstrates here.
The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan of thought. This emphasizes that Jesus' knowledge of human thoughts testifies to his divinity.
Parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus knows the scribes' thoughts and asks them why they are thinking evil in their hearts.
Parallel passage in Mark where Jesus immediately perceived in his spirit that they were reasoning thus within themselves, and asked them why they had such thoughts in their hearts.
John writes that Jesus knew all people and needed no one to testify about a person, for he himself knew what was in man—this supports Jesus' ability to read thoughts.
Jesus knew from the beginning who did not believe and who would betray him, showing his supernatural knowledge of people's inner lives.
Jesus refers to himself as the one who searches kidneys and hearts, thus linking his knowledge of human thoughts directly to the divine attribute described in the OT.
God's word judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart. The context is that nothing is hidden from God's eyes, which mirrors Jesus' insight into the Pharisees' thoughts.
